One strategy on the big screen. One screener on your laptop. Every order in the sandbox.

UAT vs PROD

Same code. Two worlds.

UAT · sandbox

  • Fake money, unlimited
  • Same API, same SDK, same dashboards
  • 100 trading ops / sec
  • Today: every order goes here
  • Mistakes cost nothing

PROD · live

  • Your money
  • Same data, same code, full price history
  • 10 trading ops / sec per IP, static IP rules
  • Today: read-only, it feeds your candles and live stream
  • Mistakes cost money
orders = InitNubraSdk(NubraEnv.UAT,  env_creds=True)   # today: every order goes here (fake money)
data   = InitNubraSdk(NubraEnv.PROD, env_creds=True)   # today: read-only, candles + the live stream
NubraTrader(data)                                       # one word from real consequences. Not today.
Sources: Nubra SDK docs (Rate Limits, Authentication, Historical Market Data: UAT holds little history, PROD holds it all); Nubra blog "What is UAT". SEBI retail-algo framework (static IP) from Session 1.

Demo · the candle-colour flip

Two candles. One rule.

  • NIFTY, 1-minute candles, only completed ones
  • Nearest expiry, ATM strike, 10 lots
  • On a flip: square off the old leg, buy the new one
  • No stop-loss, no target. A teaching toy, not advice.

What the prompt says, roughly

"Using the attached Nubra Python SDK docs, write one script: log in to UAT, stream 1-minute NIFTY candles over the WebSocket, detect red→green and green→red flips, buy the ATM CE/PE of the nearest expiry, 10 lots, square off the previous leg first, print every event."

The model writes the plumbing. You still have to understand every part, which is what the next five slides are for.

Inside the code · 1 of 5

Login once, then listen

from nubra_python_sdk.start_sdk import InitNubraSdk, NubraEnv   # the login call + the env switch
from nubra_python_sdk.ticker.websocketdata import NubraDataSocket  # the WebSocket client

nubra = InitNubraSdk(NubraEnv.UAT, env_creds=True)        # log in once; phone + MPIN from .env

def on_ohlcv_data(msg):                                      # runs on EVERY stream message
    if msg.bucket_timestamp != state["bucket"]:              # a NEW minute started…
        candle_done(state["last"])                           # …so the previous one is complete
    state["bucket"], state["last"] = msg.bucket_timestamp, msg  # remember the candle being built

socket = NubraDataSocket(client=nubra, on_ohlcv_data=on_ohlcv_data)  # hand it the callback
socket.connect()                                             # open the connection (its own thread)
socket.subscribe(["NIFTY"], data_type="ohlcv", interval="1m", exchange="NSE")  # the candle feed

The stream sends the current candle as it builds. When the bucket timestamp changes, the previous candle is finished. No polling, no refresh.

Source: SDK docs, Realtime Data → OHLCV stream (fields: open, high, low, close, bucket_timestamp = candle start; NubraDataSocket lives in nubra_python_sdk.ticker.websocketdata).
Inside the code · 2 of 5

The whole strategy is ten lines

def colour(c):                                       # one candle in, one word out
    if c.close > c.open: return "GREEN"              # closed above where it opened
    if c.close < c.open: return "RED"                # closed below where it opened
    return "FLAT"                                    # equal: ignored

def update(prev, last):                              # the last two COMPLETED candles
    before, now = colour(prev), colour(last)         # the earlier word, the newer word
    if before == "RED"   and now == "GREEN": return "CE"   # flipped up: buy the call
    if before == "GREEN" and now == "RED":   return "PE"   # flipped down: buy the put
    return None                                      # no flip, do nothing

Everything else in the file is plumbing: getting candles in, getting orders out.

Inside the code · 3 of 5

"ATM, nearest expiry" in code

md = MarketData(nubra)                                     # market-data helper, reuses the login
chain = md.option_chain("NIFTY", exchange="NSE").chain     # the whole chain
expiry = sorted(chain.all_expiries)[0]                     # nearest 'YYYYMMDD'
chain = md.option_chain("NIFTY", expiry=expiry, exchange="NSE").chain  # the chain for THAT expiry

rows = chain.ce if signal == "CE" else chain.pe            # calls or puts, per the signal
row  = next(o for o in rows if o.strike_price == chain.at_the_money_strike)  # the ATM row

ref_id, lot_size = row.ref_id, row.lot_size                # what the order needs
qty = 10 * lot_size                                        # 10 lots

Underlying in

"NIFTY", never an option symbol

ATM

the SDK tells you: at_the_money_strike

Out

a ref_id and a lot_size

Source: SDK docs, Option Chain (all_expiries, at_the_money_strike, per-row ref_id, lot_size, last_traded_price in paise).
Inside the code · 4 of 5

The order payload

price = round_to_tick(last_traded_price, tick_size)      # integer PAISE, multiple of tick

result = trader.create_order({                           # one dict = one order (docs: V3)
    "refId": ref_id,  "qty": qty,  "side": "BUY",        # which, how many, which way
    "deliveryType": "IDAY",  "priceType": "LIMIT",       # intraday product, at MY price
    "validityType": "DAY",                               # good for today only
    "isMultiLeg": False,  "executionMode": "ENTRY",      # a plain single-instrument entry
    "entryPrice": price,                                 # the limit price, in paise
    "stratTags": ["bmsit-flip-demo"],                    # one tag, hyphens only
})
order_id = result.orders[0].intentOrderId                # the id you track from now on

Paise

₹125.50 is sent as 12550

Tick size

or the exchange rejects it

Tag

Source: SDK docs, Place Single Order (V3 payload), Get Order Margin, Get Orders.
Inside the code · 5 of 5

Close the old leg, check the new one

if open_leg:                                             # bought by THIS script earlier
    place("SELL", open_leg["leg"], open_leg["qty"])      # square off first

order_id = place("BUY", new_leg, qty)                    # then the new side

status = trader.get_order(order_id)[0]                   # never assume: read it back
print(status.status, status.filledQty, status.rejectionMsg)  # what the exchange decided
  • An order is a request. The exchange decides. Read the status back.
  • Open legs live in memory: if the script dies, square off in the app.

Your project today has the same five parts. Different signal.

Your project

A quant screener

Watch

14 well-known NSE stocks: daily candles for the history, a WebSocket for right now

Measure

How stretched is each one from its own normal? One number: the z-score

Rank

A table, most stretched first, re-ranking live. Optionally, one sandbox order.

Not "this chart looks oversold". A number, across many stocks, ranked, updating.

Mean · standard deviation · z-score

How far from normal?

  • Last 20 closesOne price per trading day, the one at the bell. Twenty of them is about a month. That is the stock's "recent self".
  • Mean: the centreAdd the 20 closes, divide by 20. The price the stock keeps coming back to. The dashed line.
  • Std: the usual wobbleHow far a typical day sits from the centre. A calm stock has a small std, a jumpy one a big std. About 95% of days land inside the ±2 band.
  • z = (close − mean) / stdToday's distance from the centre, counted in wobbles. No rupees in it, so a ₹50 stock and a ₹3,000 stock compare. Below −2 is rare: "stretched low", the screener's signal.
The project, as a machine

Seven boxes, in order

LOGINPROD data · UAT orders
➜
HISTORY60 daily candles × 15
➜
MATHSmean, std, z
➜
RANKa table
➜
LIVEWebSocket, 14 symbols
➜
RISKrules first
➜
ORDERone, UAT, optional

History in

historical_data, batches of 5 symbols, 1 s apart: 60 calls a minute is the limit. Prices in paise ÷ 100.

Out

symbol · close · mean20 · std20 · z · label, sorted by z. Live, the same table keeps re-ranking.

Live in

The index stream, weight 1 per symbol. Every tick replaces today's close, z is recomputed, the table reprints every 2 s.

The order condition

Only when a stock's live z crosses down through −2 (was ≥ −2, now < −2). One order per run, qty 1, LIMIT at LTP rounded to the tick, in UAT. Then read it back.

Box 6

Risk rules are the strategy

  • Max one order per run
  • Quantity 1, always
  • No order unless z < −2
  • Never buy a stretched high
  • Each refusal prints why

Your prompt

"Using the attached Nubra Python SDK docs, write screener.py in seven numbered checkpoints: (1) log in to PROD for market data with env_creds=True, and to UAT only behind a --trade flag; (2) fetch 60 daily candles for one NSE stock with historical_data and convert paise to rupees; (3) compute the 20-day mean, standard deviation and z-score of the close; (4) loop over this watchlist in batches of 5 with a 1-second pause and print a table sorted by z; (5) subscribe to the realtime index stream for the watchlist and, on every update, replace today's close with the live price, recompute z and reprint the table every 2 seconds; (6) risk rules: at most one order per run, quantity 1, only if z < −2, never a stretched high, and print why each refusal happens; (7) behind --trade, when a stock's live z crosses down through −2, place one LIMIT BUY in UAT at the last price rounded to the tick size and read the order status back. Comment every step in plain English."

Part two

Logs are for machines. Dashboards are for you.

  • What is the strategy doing right now?
  • Which stocks are stretched, at a glance?
  • One page you can show someone who does not read Python

Remember Nubra OSS? The visual dashboards we saw there this morning. Now build one for your screener.

The prompt pattern

Structure first, then code

1 · Structure

"I want a live dashboard for this screener. What repo structure would you use? List the files and what each one does."

2 · Code

"Now give me the full code for each file, one at a time."

3 · Run

"How do I install and run it?" Then paste any error back, verbatim.

dashboard/
  app.py           # the page: table, z-score bars, one price chart with bands
  data.py          # reads the cache or the screener's live table
  indicators.py    # mean, std, z   (the same maths, in one place)
  requirements.txt # whatever the model picked: Streamlit, Dash, Flask, plain HTML…

Roughly the shape you will get, whatever the tool. Asking for structure first stops the model from writing one giant file.
